speaker: Jigar Shah
title: Jigar Shah on the DOE's Role In Accelerating The Energy Transition
question: In U.S. electricity regulation, why do investor-owned utilities keep getting approval to overbuild physical grid infrastructure instead of optimizing for lower system-wide costs?
guest: We do a lot of this modeling at the Department of Energy, but we do it on a nationwide basis, which is not that helpful on the decision-making side because the decision is made at the local level. Each state has a Public Service Commission, and that Public Service Commission is the one who makes this decision. The Public Service Commission is hugely under-resourced. They get 10,000 pages of documents from the utility, and then they have to read it all and say, 'Here are the 12 assumptions in here that we don't like.' They don't really have the ability to do all of that modeling themselves. The city of LA hired the National Renewable Energy Laboratory to do a comprehensive study called LA100, and now they're implementing it because they had independent analysis. Unless you empower Public Service Commissions to do their own independent analysis, it's hard to equip them to negotiate with the utility. Remember, utilities are not bad people, but they've been given a monopoly license, and their shareholders get paid based on how much iron they put in the ground. The more money they invest, the more shareholder equity returns they make.

points.core: Regulated utilities earn shareholder returns proportional to the physical capital they deploy.
points.note: Accept: rate-of-return or cost-of-service monopoly incentives ('putting iron in the ground' or expanding the rate base) that reward higher capex over lower-cost efficiency. Do not credit: generic claims that utilities are greedy or corrupt without naming the capex-linked return structure.

points.core: Grid investment approvals happen at under-resourced state utility commissions rather than federally.
points.note: Accept: state Public Service Commissions or PUCs holding approval authority while being severely understaffed and overwhelmed by massive utility filings. Do not credit: blaming federal policy or Congress alone.

points.core: State regulators lack independent technical modeling capacity to challenge utility planning assumptions.
points.note: Accept: inability of PSCs to run their own system-wide grid models (or needing outside labs like NREL) to counter utility-supplied analyses in rate cases. Do not credit: generic calls for stricter regulation or oversight without the analytical and modeling asymmetry.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core reason is cost-of-service regulation: investor-owned utilities earn their profit as a regulated rate of return on capital invested (the "rate base"), while operating expenses, fuel, and purchased power are passed through to customers with no markup. This creates a capital bias, known as the Averch-Johnson effect: whenever the authorized return on equity exceeds the utility's true cost of capital, which evidence suggests it commonly does, building more poles, wires, and plants raises shareholder earnings, whereas cheaper alternatives like efficiency, demand response, grid-enhancing technologies, or buying from third parties earn little or nothing.

Regulators approve these plans for several reasons. Utilities hold a large information advantage over understaffed commissions and consumer advocates, and they control the planning models and data. Reliability arguments are hard to rebut, since commissioners face blame for blackouts but little for gradual rate increases. Local transmission projects often escape competitive bidding and rigorous review. Utilities also wield substantial political and lobbying influence.

That said, "overbuild" is contested: some spending reflects genuine aging-asset replacement, load growth, and resilience needs. Reforms like performance-based regulation try to realign the incentives.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Investor-owned utilities overbuild physical infrastructure primarily because traditional cost-of-service regulation rewards capital spending over operational efficiency, a capital bias known as the Averch-Johnson effect. Utilities earn a shareholder return only on physical assets added to their rate base, such as substations and power lines, whereas operational solutions like grid-enhancing software, demand response, or purchased power are merely passed through at cost without a profit margin.

Regulators keep approving these capital-heavy plans due to information asymmetry, skewed political incentives, and fragmented oversight. Utilities control the proprietary grid data, load forecasts, and engineering models used to define system needs, leaving understaffed state utility commissions poorly equipped to prove that cheaper non-wires alternatives would work. Meanwhile, commissioners face immediate political backlash if reliability falters, whereas the cost of excess hardware is amortized quietly across ratepayers over decades. Furthermore, many local transmission upgrades are recovered through federal formula rates that update automatically, largely bypassing state prudency reviews and system-wide cost optimization.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The main reason is cost-of-service, rate-of-return regulation. Utilities earn an authorized return on capital they invest, their "rate base." They usually recover operating expenses only at cost, with no profit. So a substation, transmission line, or new feeder earns money for shareholders, while a cheaper option often earns nothing. Those cheaper options include grid-enhancing technologies like dynamic line ratings, demand response, efficiency, distributed storage, and buying services from third parties. Economists call this capital bias the Averch-Johnson effect. It's worse when authorized returns on equity sit above the utility's actual cost of capital, which many analysts argue has been true for years.

Regulators approve these projects for structural reasons. The utility controls the grid data and the planning models. Commission staff are small compared with utility teams. Reviews look at whether each project is "prudent" rather than whether it's the cheapest way to meet system needs. Reliability failures are politically costly, so regulators lean toward more hardware. Local "supplemental" transmission projects also get little competitive or regional review.

"Overbuild" is a contested label, since load growth and aging equipment are real. Reforms try to fix the incentives through performance-based ratemaking, letting utilities earn returns on cloud services and other operating expenses, and independent planning.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Under traditional U.S. cost-of-service regulation, investor-owned utilities earn their regulated profits almost exclusively as a percentage return on their "rate base"—the physical capital assets they own, such as transmission lines, substations, and power plants. Operational expenses, including software, grid-enhancing technologies, demand response, or third-party power contracts, are typically passed through to customers at cost with no profit margin. This structural capital bias, known as the Averch–Johnson effect, gives utilities a direct financial incentive to favor expensive physical construction over cheaper operational or non-wires alternatives.

These projects repeatedly win approval because of severe information asymmetry and misaligned incentives at state public utility commissions. Utilities control the grid data, load forecasts, and engineering models, while under-resourced regulators often lack the technical capacity to independently test lower-cost alternatives. Moreover, both regulators and utilities face harsh political backlash for blackouts but far less immediate accountability for incremental rate hikes, creating a shared bias toward conservative overbuilding within each utility’s own territory rather than optimizing costs across the wider grid.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
U.S. electricity regulation gives investor-owned utilities a financial reason to build. Under cost-of-service regulation, utilities generally recover the cost of approved grid investments from customers and earn a return on the portion still in the rate base. Many cheaper alternatives, such as paying customers to shift demand away from peak hours, are treated as operating expenses. The utility can recover those costs, but it typically earns no comparable return.

Regulators can reject unnecessary projects, but they often rely on the utility’s own forecasts and engineering analysis to judge what’s needed. Approving extra capacity can look like the safer choice when outages draw immediate scrutiny and the costs of overbuilding are spread across customer bills for decades. Planning and approval are also split across utilities, states, and regional bodies, so a project can satisfy a local reliability requirement even when a coordinated solution would cost less across the system.

noweb.answer:
Investor-owned utilities generally earn an authorized return on approved capital investments. A new substation or transmission line can increase earnings for years, while cheaper options such as demand response or better use of existing lines often offer less financial upside. Customers typically pay for approved projects through their rates, so the utility has a weaker incentive to minimize total system costs.

Regulators can reject unnecessary spending, but utilities usually have more detailed information about their own grids and develop the forecasts that justify new projects. The risks are also asymmetric. An outage can draw immediate scrutiny, while the cost of excess capacity is spread across customers’ bills for years. And when the costs and benefits of a cheaper alternative fall across different utilities, states, or customer groups, no single decision-maker may have the authority or incentive to choose it. Together, those incentives make building easier to propose and easier to approve.

The central reason is that investor-owned utilities generally earn a regulated return on approved capital investments. A new substation can increase earnings for years. Using demand response to defer that substation may save customers more money, but the utility typically receives little of the savings. Regulators review whether spending is prudent, yet a project can look reasonable on its own even when a cheaper alternative exists.

Utilities also develop the demand forecasts and identify the reliability needs that shape many proposals. Regulators face an asymmetry: if they approve excess capacity, the cost is spread across customer bills for years. If they defer a project and an outage follows, the consequences are immediate and visible. And because authority is split among state commissions, federal regulators, and regional grid operators, the entity approving a project may see only part of its system-wide costs and benefits. Together, those incentives favor construction even when a lower-cost option could deliver the same reliability.
